author: Wagner
title: No more Isolde
where: *Tristan und Isolde*, Act 2, Scenes 1 and 2, and the end of Act 3
about: Tristan is bringing the Irish princess Isolde by ship to Cornwall, to marry his uncle, King Mark. She orders a death potion for the two of them, and her maid Brangäne pours a love potion in its place. In Act 2 Isolde waits for Tristan at night in a garden, and they sing together until Mark surprises them at dawn. In Act 3 Tristan, wounded by the king’s man Melot, dies as Isolde reaches him, and she sings over his body.

view.says: Summing up de Rougemont in 1941, Auden calls the Tristan legend, which Wagner’s opera crowns, the chief form of a myth in which perfection comes only by death: for the lovers, love lasts in time only while something bars its consummation, and only death can make them one. Speaking for himself, he adds that their tie holds no possibilities, fixed as it is to a thing already done, the potion they drank.
view.quote: something predestined, for which they have no moral responsibility
view.source: “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941, a review of Denis de Rougemont’s *Love in the Western World*; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 138 and 140

plates.heading: Whose work
plates.label: Wagner

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: Brangäne has blamed herself for Isolde’s shame. Isolde’s answer begins Dein Werk?, your work? In its last fourteen lines short brackets mark the verb of each clause, ten (one in two words), and long ones show whose they are. Two are Isolde’s, both past: she nahm, took, death’s work in hand, and ward, became, another’s own. Seven are Frau Minne’s, Lady Love’s, from past to what may come: has taken away, took, grasped, turns, ends, may choose, may lead. The tenth orders the maid to let her obey. Auden wrote in 1941 that the lovers’ tie holds no possibilities: it is fixed to a thing already done, the potion they drank.
lenses.why: Of the ten verbs two are Isolde’s, both past, and seven are Lady Love’s, who took the deed, turns it and may lead her. Auden in 1941: the lovers’ tie holds no possibilities, being fixed to the potion they drank.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. Brangäne’s words stand [just before this speech](#/read/tristan/act-2:25). The verbs and their forms: the DWDS dictionary under *nehmen*, *werden*, *entwenden*, *fassen*, *wenden*, *enden*, *küren* and *führen*; the form for what may be, the present subjunctive: English Wikipedia, “Subjunctive mood.” Auden: “Eros and Agape” (1941), in *Prose*, vol. II, pp. 139–40.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Werk, work, and Hand end the two lines of Isolde’s own act. Six lines later the same two words end the lines in which Lady Love has the work in her hand. In between, Hand rhymes with entwandt, taken away, and Pfand, pledge. The dotted letters are alliteration, the device of Wagner’s Ring poems: one first sound joins Minne, Love, to meiner Macht, my power, which she takes the work from. Auden set this speech’s opening words over his pages on these lovers and their servants, and wrote there that the exchange of potions binds the two from outside, not by their own decisions.
lenses.why: The end words work and hand close Isolde’s own act and come back as Lady Love’s, with taken away and pledge rhymed between; Auden wrote that something outside the two binds them, and that they are not answerable for it.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. The rhyme words: their sounds in the DWDS dictionary under *Hand* and German Wiktionary under *Pfand* and *gewandt*, their senses in the DWDS dictionary under *entwenden* and *Pfand*. Alliteration, and Wagner’s *Ring* poems written in it: English Wikipedia, “Alliteration” and “Alliterative verse.” Auden: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 118 and 122.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: *Werk* is a deed as well as a thing made. The noun stands six times in the libretto: once in Brangäne’s cry in Act 1 at what she has done, and five times here, in Brangäne’s speech and Isolde’s answer.
*Vermessen* is an elevated word for one who presumes too far: overbold, arrogant.
To take a thing *zur Hand* is to take it up for use, as one takes up a tool or a book.

*Minne* is a knight’s courtly service of a revered lady in the Middle Ages, and an old word for love. It fell out of use in the sixteenth century and came back in the eighteenth with the study of the medieval poets.
*Entwenden* is an elevated word for taking a thing from someone; it can mean to steal. Luther’s Bible uses this verb where God takes a father’s goods from him and gives them to another.

*Weihen* is to consecrate, as a priest or a church is consecrated; *dem Tode geweiht* is said of one who cannot escape death. In Act 1, her eyes on Tristan, Isolde says this line’s word twice: a head and a heart devoted to death.
A *Pfand* is a thing a creditor holds as security for a debt. Grimm’s dictionary notes that a person too can be taken as a pledge, like a surety or a hostage.

notes.gloss: what she may choose for me
notes.note: *Küren* is an elevated word for choosing or electing. A related word, *erkoren*, chosen, is Isolde’s word in Act 1, her eyes on Tristan: chosen for me, lost to me.
*Eigen* is what belongs to someone. Of persons it once meant unfree: a lord’s bondman was his *eigen*. Grimm’s dictionary adds that the word is also said of lovers.

*Gehorsam* is the following of commands. Its adjective, *gehorsam*, arose, the dictionary says, to render the Latin for a Christian’s obedience to God and the clergy. Wagner’s poem as printed in 1873 and the vocal score have the adjective here, with a small *g*.

lenses.caption: The small glosses give the plain sense. Minne is the love of the medieval poets, who address it as a lady, Frau Minne. Isolde speaks of her in words of debt and lordship: taken in Pfand, as the pledge a creditor holds; become zu eigen, her own, a word once used of bondmen; owing Gehorsam, obedience, whose adjective arose to render the Latin for a Christian’s obedience to God. Earlier in the speech Love is a queen, with life and death her subjects. The myth, Auden wrote in 1948, could only arise where people are taught that to give oneself to God is a free and absolute commitment.
lenses.why: Isolde’s words for Lady Love are of pledge, ownership and obedience, a word whose adjective arose for obedience to God; Auden: the myth needed a society taught that giving the self to God is a free and absolute act.
lenses.stands: The German words: the DWDS dictionary under *Minne*, *Pfand*, *eigen*, *Gehorsam*, *entwenden*, *vermessen*, *weihen* and *küren*, with Wolfgang Pfeifer’s etymologies there, and Grimm’s dictionary under *minne*, *frau*, *pfand*, *eigen* and *entwenden*. *Frau Minne* in the medieval poets: English Wikipedia, “Frau Minne.” The queen with life and death as her subjects: [earlier in this speech](#/read/tristan/act-2:27). Auden: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 25.

plates.heading: Two names
plates.label: Wagner

lenses.label: Crossing
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order; here pronoun and name, then name and pronoun
lenses.caption: This German text gives Isolde the first three lines and Tristan the next three; in the vocal score he answers each as it ends. She calls him Du, you, by her own name, takes his name for ich, I, and drops her own: nicht mehr, no more. He does the same. Pronoun and name change places from line to line, a crossing, with no verb between them and no und, the “and” Isolde earlier calls a sweet little word. Each addresses the other as the singer’s self. Auden told the 1941 class, a student recalled, that romantic lovers are narcissists, each finding in the other the proof of being exceptional.
lenses.why: Each gives the other the singer’s own name, then drops it; pronoun and name cross with no verb and no “and” between. Auden told the 1941 class, by a student’s account, that romantic lovers are narcissists.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage; chiasmus as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Who sings which lines: the German text of *Die Musikdramen* (1971) and the vocal score, pp. 174–75; a libretto of 1906 prints Tristan’s lines first, bracketed with Isolde’s. Isolde on the word *und*: earlier in the scene, in lines the English leaves out. Auden in class: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan” (1985), pp. 137–38.

lenses.label: Grammar

spans.label: a verb used as a noun
a verb used as a noun
a verb used as a noun
a verb used as a noun

lenses.caption: In the last eight lines every word is marked by its kind: sixteen words, and not one verb that tells who does a thing or when. Four verbs stand as nouns, with capitals: naming, parting, knowing, catching fire. A verb in that form shows no person and no tense. The lines set phrase beside phrase, and endlos ewig, endlessly, eternally, is two words of like meaning. Auden noted in 1969 that in Tristan Wagner strings together phrases set side by side and words of like meaning as his music needs them, and in 1962 that the passion of the two has nothing before or after it but itself.
lenses.why: The last eight lines have no verb with person or tense: four verbs are nouns, telling neither who acts nor when. Auden: Wagner strings phrases together as his music needs; the passion has nothing before or after it but itself.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A verb form without person or tense: English Wikipedia, “Nonfinite verb”; that form used as a noun in German: “German verbs” and “German nouns” there. The words: the DWDS dictionary under *nennen*, *trennen*, *erkennen*, *entbrennen*, *endlos* and *ewig*. Auden: “The Greatest of the Monsters” (1969), in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 252; “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 121.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: In this German text each name rhymes only with itself; Isolde’s lines and Tristan’s share one rhyme, ich, I. The libretto gives the last eight lines to both: four on one rhyme, then ein-bewußt, aware as one, rhymed with Brust, breast, and Liebeslust, love’s delight. In the vocal score Isolde alone sings the four, and the voices join only in the last line. Auden told the 1941 class, a student recalled, that Wagner keeps the lovers’ voices from unison until the duet’s end, and that their lives are to go the same way.
lenses.why: As printed, her lines and his share one rhyme, the word for I; the lines given to both run on two rhymes, and the score keeps the voices apart until the last. Auden: these two want two souls made one.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The sounds: German Wiktionary under *bewusst* and *Lust*, the DWDS dictionary under *Brust*, Grimm’s dictionary under *bewust*. Who sings which lines: the German text of *Die Musikdramen* (1971), a libretto of 1906 and the vocal score, pp. 174–78. Auden in class: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan” (1985), p. 138.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: *Namenlos*, Tristan’s word earlier in the scene, means nameless and, in elevated use, beyond telling. The English printed here leaves the word out.
*Trennen* is to undo what joins two things or two people. Tristan’s sentence earlier in the scene has *ungetrennt*, undivided.
*Erkennen* is to perceive and to recognize. In Luther’s Bible it is also the verb for a man’s knowing a woman: Adam knew his wife.
*Entbrennen* is to catch fire. Grimm’s dictionary cites it from Luther’s Bible for a heart that takes fire with feeling.
*Ein* is the numeral one; *bewusst* is aware, conscious. Grimm’s dictionary has no entry for the compound.
*Lust* is desire and the pleasure of having it met. English *lust* is the same word; its sense narrowed to sinful desire through Bible translations, while the German word kept the sense of pleasure.

lenses.caption: Earlier in the scene Tristan speaks of dying so as to live undivided and namenlos, nameless. The close takes up both: ohne Nennen, without naming, ohne Trennen, without parting. What remains is Erkennen, a knowing, in Luther’s Bible the word for a man’s knowing a woman, and Entbrennen, a catching fire, both new. Auden thought Wagner probably meant the duet to stand for the physical act; what an audience sees, he wrote, is two singers telling of their desire, and if the two gave way they would come to know something of each other.
lenses.why: The close names a knowing with no naming in it, in the Bible’s word for a man’s knowing a woman; Auden held that if the two gave way they would come to know something of each other.
lenses.stands: The German words: the DWDS dictionary under *nennen*, *namenlos*, *trennen*, *erkennen*, *entbrennen*, *bewusst* and *Lust*; Grimm’s dictionary under *erkennen* and *entbrennen*; the Online Etymology Dictionary under *lust*. Tristan on dying undivided: [earlier in the scene](#/read/tristan/act-2:76), where the English leaves out the word for nameless. Auden: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 122.

plates.heading: The last twelve lines
plates.label: Wagner

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: Isolde’s last questions hang on Soll ich, shall I. Sollen is the verb for what another’s will requires; in a question put to oneself it tells of indecision. This is her last verb that says who acts, and mich, myself, three lines on, is her last word for herself. After that line there is no pronoun and no question mark: three phrases beginning with in, two bare verbs, drown and sink, then unbewußt, unconscious, and a cry. Auden wrote in 1941 that when Eros, the will of every creature to realize itself, tries to live only in what might be, the end, if not sickness, is the physical world breaking in and destroying consciousness; his next sentence is about Tristan.
lenses.why: Her last verb with a person asks what she is to do; then eight lines with no pronoun, no such verb. Auden, 1941: when Eros hides in the possible the end, if not sickness, is the physical world destroying consciousness.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. The verb *sollen*: the DWDS dictionary, senses 1 and 2 b. The other words: the DWDS dictionary under *ertrinken*, *versinken* and *unbewusst*. Auden: “Eros and Agape” (1941), in *Prose*, vol. II, pp. 139–40.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Three rhyme words lose a consonant at each step: Schwall, a surge as of water, Schall, sound, All, the universe. The last two lines have the rhyme that closed the first lines given to both lovers in Act 1 and their duet in Act 2: there, you alone known to me; then, aware as one; here, unbewußt, unaware: the same word with un- before it, the German for unconscious. The last line is theirs too, less the word for love: höchste Lust, highest delight. Each one’s passion, Auden wrote, aims past the other at Nirvana, a unity before anything was many.
lenses.why: The rhyme words shrink from surge to sound to the All, and the last rhyme is that of the lovers’ first lines and of their duet, now on unaware. Auden: their passion aims past each other at Nirvana.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The rhyme words: their sounds in German Wiktionary under *Schwall*, *Schall*, *All*, *unbewusst* and *Lust*, their senses in the DWDS dictionary under the same words. The same rhyme earlier: [the first lines given to both lovers](#/read/tristan/act-1:335) and [the end of the duet](#/read/tristan/act-2:122), in the German of both. Auden: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 122.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: short lines of one or two beats: four syllables in the questions, then two lines of six, one of five, one of four and four of three

points.say: Six syllables. This line and the next are the longest in the song, and each begins with two unstressed syllables.
Three syllables and one beat: a single word is the whole line.

lenses.caption: The rule under each line is its measure; the dots are the spoken stresses. The four lines of questions have four syllables each, like twenty-one of the twenty-two lines before them. After the last question the measure changes: two lines of six syllables, the only ones in the song, each beginning off the beat; then one of five, one of four and four of three. The two long lines name the surge and the sound; three of the shortest are single words: drown, sink, unconscious. The line a composer writes for the voice, Auden held, is decided by the syllables of the words. With Chester Kallman he wrote that Wagner insisted on a text that matched his musical ideas exactly.
lenses.why: The four-syllable line of the questions breaks after the last question mark: six, six, five, four, then four lines of three. Auden held that a composer’s vocal line is decided by the syllables of the words.
lenses.stands: The stresses are one reader’s hearing of the lines said aloud; the syllables are counted in the German printed here. Where the stress falls in *untertauchen* and *unbewusst*: the DWDS dictionary and German Wiktionary. The senses of *Schwall*, *Schall*, *ertrinken*, *versinken* and *unbewusst*: the DWDS dictionary. Auden: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 473; with Chester Kallman, “Translating Opera Libretti,” in the same book, p. 489.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: *Verhauchen* is an elevated, veiled word for breathing out one’s life: Isolde asks whether to breathe herself away. In the English she wins the breezes to her own breathing.
A *Schwall* is a great mass, above all of water, that breaks over one like a wave. The English has *breezes*.
*All* is the universe. In medieval German the word was said of God, and later of a beloved person. The English has a *whirlwind*.
*Unbewußt*, unconscious, has no word in the English. In its place the singer is drinking *in a kiss*.
*Lust* is desire and its pleasure in one word. *Bliss* keeps the pleasure, and *kiss* in the line before rhymes with it.

lenses.caption: Under each German line stands the English that H. and F. Corder fitted to the vocal score. It keeps each line’s syllable count and the scheme of the rhymes, and changes what is said. Isolde asks whether to breathe herself away; the English Isolde draws the breezes in. Unbewußt, unconscious, is left out: where it stood the singer is drinking in a kiss. Wagner’s last eight lines name no kiss and no person. Auden held that in song a listener hears syllables, not words, and that Wagner in English is intolerable, and would be even if the English were better verse than the German, since the new syllables do not fit the notes.
lenses.why: The English keeps every line’s syllable count and the rhyme scheme and changes the sense: for unconscious it has a kiss. Auden held that song is heard as syllables, and that Wagner in English is intolerable.
lenses.stands: The two texts, line under line. The German words: the DWDS dictionary under *verhauchen*, *Schwall*, *All*, *unbewusst* and *Lust*, with Wolfgang Pfeifer’s note on *All*. The translators, and their English under the music: the Breitkopf & Härtel vocal score, title page and pp. 274–76. Auden: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 473.

auden.says: The 1941 class, as the student Donald Pearce recalled it, was set *Romeo and Juliet*, the librettos of *Carmen* and *Tristan und Isolde*, and de Rougemont’s new book. Auden made two points, much on de Rougemont’s lines: that romantic lovers are narcissists, and that their love needs a barrier, at best one that cannot be overcome, so that only death can unite them. What such lovers love, he said, is death. Then he played the love duet on a phonograph.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 137–39

auden.says: Auden’s review of 1941, summing up de Rougemont, sets the legend of Don Juan beside that of Tristan as its opposite, a legend that says yes to the flesh and no to the spirit and lives for the present moment alone. To Tristan time is an ill to be borne and to Don Juan an ill to be smashed, so Auden names the one a suicide and the other a murderer. Neither knows the one he loves as a person. Opposed to both alike, he writes, is what Christianity teaches about Agape; a page later he calls it Eros changed by grace.
auden.source: “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 138–39

auden.says: Later in the same review Auden speaks for himself. Eros, for him the basic will of every creature to realize itself, must in man make the possible actual by deciding, and runs from that task in two ways. Hiding in the actual, it gets, unless madness comes, the opposite of what it sought: possibilities break in and destroy the actual, and Don Juan’s affairs stay possibilities never made real. Hiding in the possible, it finds, unless sickness comes, the physical world breaking in upon consciousness: Tristan’s tie to Isolde, fixed to a thing already done, holds no possibilities. He asks what can free man so that Eros dares to decide.
auden.source: “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 139–40

auden.says: In a lecture of September 1940 Auden explains why Wagner is popular: ordinary people afraid for their jobs do feel held by a fate beyond their control and, like Tristan, are glad of night and its dreams after a dull day’s work. Suffering, he goes on, is what Wagner’s art could voice, and in Tristan and Isolde it is the pain of self-love. His best passages, he adds, are for one voice alone. In a review of June 1941 he writes that sex was a torment to Wagner, and that nothing is less a matter of biology, or more a matter of the mind, than Tristan and Isolde’s love.
auden.source: “Mimesis and Allegory,” a lecture given at Columbia University on 14 September 1940 and printed in *English Institute Annual 1940* (1941), and “Ambiguous Answers,” *The New Republic*, 23 June 1941, a review of Jacques Barzun’s *Darwin, Marx, Wagner*; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 83 and 136

auden.says: In 1944, setting out Kierkegaard’s three ways of judging, Auden takes these lovers as his case. In betraying Mark the two feel guilt, yet thwarted desire would have hurt them more had they kept their vows. The aesthetic view wants all three to suffer, because that makes the situation interesting. The ethical view would have them keep faith and would gladly swap the love potion for a strong sedative, since it cares only how they act. The religious view has a blessing for them only to the degree that their guilt is truly suffered, and blesses Mark most, whose suffering is the more innocent and who, belatedly, forgives.
auden.source: “A Preface to Kierkegaard,” *The New Republic*, 15 May 1944, a review of *Either/Or*; in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 215–16

auden.says: In 1948 Auden calls the story one of two modern erotic myths with no parallel in Greek literature; the other is Don Juan. The potion, where the story has one, only makes the two see that they already love, and take the fact as fated and beyond recall. Each holds the other as the highest good, and still their bond is a torment: desire is only the sign of a longing to become one, which bodies forbid, so that the end they seek is to die embracing. The potion and the obstacle that cannot be removed guard them against change.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 23–25

auden.says: In *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden calls it lucky for an understanding of the myth that Wagner made an opera of it: a stout tenor and soprano cannot be taken for a pair drawn together by good looks. The two are mythical figures, never met in life, and each is so indifferent to who the other is that, he says, they might as well have been paired by lot. Elsewhere in the book he counts them among the great operatic roles, each a state of passion and will, and holds that a music-drama needs a libretto with nothing sensible said in it, which is hard to bring off, though Wagner did.
auden.quote: their passion is not for each other but for something they hope to obtain by means of each other
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” pp. 120–22, and “Notes on Music and Opera,” pp. 470 and 472, in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962)

auden.says: Reviewing a life of Wagner in 1969, Auden agrees with its author that Wagner’s affair with Mathilde Wesendonk came out of this opera and did not cause it. A close reader of its words and music, he says, becomes aware of a homosexual triangle of Mark, Melot and Tristan: when the lovers are caught, Mark’s long speech passes over Isolde and is spoken to Tristan alone. He also sets the opera against the theory Wagner published in 1851, which ruled out duets, repeated words, strict meters and even rhyme: in *Tristan* the duet comes back and the orchestra drowns the words.
auden.source: “The Greatest of the Monsters,” *The New Yorker*, 4 January 1969, a review of Robert Gutman’s *Richard Wagner: The Man, His Mind, and His Music*; in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 247–48 and 251–52

sources: The text: Richard Wagner, *Tristan und Isolde* (the poem first printed in Leipzig in 1859; first performed in Munich on 10 June 1865), in the German that zeno.org gives from *Die Musikdramen* (Hamburg, 1971). caveats: The view that opens the page is mostly Auden’s 1941 summary of de Rougemont’s thesis; its last sentence, and his essays of 1948 and 1962, are in his own voice. Apart from the duet and the words set over his essay, no remark of his on these passages was found.

What Auden said in class in 1941 comes from an account that a student, Donald Pearce, wrote long after. It is not Auden’s own text, and what he said of the duet concerns the music, which this page does not show.

In the vocal score Tristan answers each of Isolde’s lines with pronoun and name the other way around, so the two share her name at a line’s end, not the word for I. Wagner’s poem as printed in 1873 and the English libretto have four lines of names, for both.
The stresses marked are one reader’s hearing of lines written to be sung. The first word of the first line and the word for myself in the fourth can fairly be given more weight or less.
Auden’s pieces of 1940, 1941 and 1944 were read only in search results of a scanned copy, with page numbers taken from the nearest running heads.
